paras: The Eighth Avenue crowd pursuit of George Smith took place in Manhattan on the night of about 11 June 1903, when white men chased Smith, a 19-year-old Black man accused of insulting a woman and slashing her escort with a razor. Police arrested Smith, and he was held on a charge of felonious assault. The Evening World put the crowd at about 500 and described the episode as "almost a race riot."

According to the Evening World, Robert Russell, 32, was escorting a young woman home from the American Theatre when Smith allegedly insulted her at Thirty-seventh Street. The Sun instead placed the encounter at Thirty-ninth Street and said Smith had insulted two women walking with Russell.

In the Evening World's account, Russell turned back to resent the remark, and Smith allegedly drew a razor and cut him slightly about the shoulder. The Sun reported that Russell "started to thrash the negro" first, and that the razor cut only Russell's clothes. A crowd of white men then joined Russell in chasing Smith up Eighth Avenue.

Smith ran into the arms of Policeman Muthall, and the crowd, said to number about 500, wanted to take him from the officer. The Evening World said Muthall nonetheless locked Smith up "without trouble," while the Sun wrote that "things were going hard with him" until two policemen arrested him and drove the crowd off.
The next day Smith was held in the West Side Court on a charge of felonious assault. Neither account reports an arrest of anyone in the crowd, and no report of the outcome of Smith's case was found.

Two New York dailies carried short items on 12 June 1903, both told from Russell's side. The Evening World headlined it "Almost a Race Riot in Street Assault" and qualified the charges as "alleged," while the Sun's deck, "He'd Insulted Two Women and Slashed Their Escort With a Razor," stated them as fact. Both papers identified Smith by race and the pursuers as "white men," and neither questioned the crowd's chase. No Black-press coverage of the incident was found.

bases: A crowd of white men chased George Smith after an alleged razor attack, and "things were going hard with him" until police intervened (A2), with about 500 people wanting to take him from a policeman (A1); no injury to Smith is reported.
Two New York papers with differently worded, independently detailed reports (A1, A2) agree that a crowd of white men chased Smith on Eighth Avenue until police arrested him.

accounts.label: Evening World report
accounts.gist: Smith allegedly insulted a young woman Russell was escorting home from the American Theatre, slashed Russell when he turned back, and fled; a crowd of about 500 wanted to take him from Policeman Muthall, who locked him up without trouble.

accounts.label: Sun report
accounts.gist: Smith insulted two women walking with Russell; Russell started to thrash him and Smith slashed with a razor, cutting only Russell's clothes; two policemen arrested Smith and drove off the pursuing crowd.

framing.detail: The Evening World headlined "Almost a Race Riot in Street Assault" and hedged the charges with "alleged," but presented the crowd's pursuit as following from Smith's insult and attack.
The Sun's headline "Crowd Chases a Negro" stated the insult and slashing as fact in its deck ("He'd Insulted Two Women"), while noting that "things were going hard with him" until police intervened.

quotes: A negro's alleged assault on a white man who resented a remark made by the negro nearly caused a race riot in Eighth avenue.
The crowd, numbering about 500, wanted to take the colored man from the policeman, but the latter locked him up without trouble.
